previous_admission_summary.summary_paragraph: The patient was admitted for a one-week history of burning epigastric pain, coffee-ground emesis, and melena, in the setting of chronic pancreatitis, Sjogren’s syndrome, and ongoing prednisone use for presumed vasculitis. Her symptoms differed from prior pancreatitis episodes, with no radiation to the back and normal lipase. Initial labs showed a drop in hemoglobin from 12.1 to 10.2 g/dL, suggesting gastrointestinal blood loss. She was managed with IV fluids, famotidine (due to IV PPI allergy), and pain control with Dilaudid. An endoscopy revealed normal mucosa in the esophagus, stomach, and duodenum with no active bleeding or ulcers. The proton pump inhibitor was increased to pantoprazole 40 mg twice daily. Her condition stabilized, pain improved, and she was discharged home on hospital day three with instructions to follow up with gastroenterology and to return if symptoms recurred.
problems: Dyspepsia and other specified disorders of function of stomach

Brief Hospital Course:
The patient was admitted to the medical service with abdominal 
pain and a report of tarry black stools. She refused an NG 
lavage in the emergency department. Her rectal exam was guiac 
negative. She received zofran and dilaudid for pain. She had 
hematocrit's that remained stable over time. She coudl not take 
po for several days. On the day of discharge her pain was 
manageable with oral medications and she was tolerating oral 
intake. She was discharged with follow up.

Her abdominal pain was without clear etiology. Given her normal 
EGD 1 week prior, no interventions or imaging was obtained. Her 
course was self-limited, possibly of viral etiology. Concerning, 
of course, is her continued rate of admissions and need for 
narcotic medications. She wished to be discharged prior to her 
being set up with an outpatient pain psychologist. This 
intervention was recommended to her.
